pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2). Solve one-step WORD PROBLEMS involving addition and subtraction to 20, INCLUDING missing-number problems (7 = ? − 9). Extends within-10 modelling to a larger range and, importantly, to problems where the unknown is not the result.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'solve one-step problems that involve addition and subtraction… and missing number problems such as 7 = ? − 9'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.1 'use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems… with unknowns in all positions'; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
• Operational details — Continue modelling the SITUATION (act out / draw / bar model) rather than keyword-matching, now with numbers to 20 and with the unknown in the start, change or result position. Missing-number problems are the key new demand: the child must represent an unknown and reason to it, often using the inverse or a known bond. Bar/part-whole models become powerful here for making the unknown visible.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): solve result-unknown add/subtract problems to 20 by modelling. Tier B (age 6): solve change-unknown problems and simple missing-number equations with support. Tier C (age 6-7): solve start-unknown and missing-number problems (7 = ? − 9), explaining the model and using the inverse to find the unknown.
bestPractices: Keep teaching modelling of the situation (act-out, drawing, bar/part-whole) over keyword strategies, extending to numbers to 20.
Introduce the unknown in all positions (result, change, start) and use part-whole/bar models to make the unknown visible so children can reason to it.
Connect missing-number problems to the inverse relationship and to known bonds (7 = ? − 9 → ? = 16 via 7 + 9).
Have children write the equation that matches the situation, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after =).
Progress difficulty by problem structure, not just larger numbers, and discuss why a chosen model fits the story.
keyRepresentations: Bar/tape model showing known parts and an unknown
Part-part-whole model with the unknown in any slot
Objects/drawings acted on to match the story
Empty number line for counting on to find a difference/unknown
Equations with a box/letter for the unknown in varied positions
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching (fails on missing-number and compare problems).
Assuming the unknown is always the result, so start- and change-unknown problems stump them.
Rejecting missing-number forms because = is read as 'answer here'.
Combining the two given numbers regardless of the structure (e.g. adding in a start-unknown problem that needs subtraction).
Not using the inverse/known bond to find the unknown, instead guessing.

learn.summary: For ages 5-7 (Y1/early Y2): solve one-step word problems involving addition and subtraction to 20, including missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9. The core objective is modelling the situation (acting out, drawing, bar/part-whole models) rather than keyword-matching, and crucially handling problems where the unknown sits in the start, change or result position — not only the answer slot. Bar/part-whole models make the unknown visible so children can reason to it using the inverse or a known bond.

activities.title: Story-to-bar-model builder
feedback: Check the structure of the model, not just the final number: does the bar place the known parts and the unknown where the story puts them?

If the pieces dragged in don't match the story — for example a given whole treated as a part, or both numbers entered as parts when one of them is actually the whole — ask them to re-read it event by event: 'What was there to begin with? What happened? What is left?'
For 7 = ? − 9, prompt: 'We start with a mystery number, take away 9, and 7 are left — so the mystery number is 9 and 7 put together, 16.'

Praise correctly reasoning to an unknown via the inverse or a known bond, and show how the model did the work: adding the parts to find a missing whole, or taking a known part from the whole to find a missing part.
activities.rationale: The skill is modelling situations with the unknown in varied positions; a build-your-own bar/part-whole model lets the child place the unknown and manipulate it so the inverse is made visible, with varied problem structures generated across a session. An interactive model can rotate the unknown position and give feedback on the structure of the model, which a fixed worked example cannot do, though a fixed example can still illustrate the method. Proposed design; efficacy not independently verified.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
1.OA.1: use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems with unknowns in all positions; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
Bar/part-whole modelling makes the unknown visible and supports reasoning (including via the inverse) across all unknown positions; keyword strategies fail on missing-number problems.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a one-step problem with numbers to 20, e.g. 'I had some sweets, ate 9, and 7 are left.'
Drag the quantities you know into a bar or part-whole frame — for this story, split a whole into a '9 eaten' part and a '7 left' part.
Mark where the unknown sits in the model (here the WHOLE — the number you started with — is the mystery).
Act on the model to find the unknown — combine the two parts to fill the whole (7 + 9 = 16), or count on along a number line.
Repeat with problems that rotate the unknown through result, change and start positions, and with pure missing-number equations like 7 = ? − 9.
Write the equation that matches your model, placing the unknown where it belongs (not always after the = sign).
activities.intendedInsight: A problem where the unknown is the START or the CHANGE, not the answer, is not impossible: the bar model shows exactly where the mystery sits. If the unknown is the whole, combining the known parts finds it. If the unknown is a part, taking the known part away from the whole (or counting on from it) finds it. Children learn to model any structure rather than hope a keyword tells them what to do.

activities.title: Hands-on modelling with counters, drawings and paper bars
feedback: If the model and story disagree, re-read the story one event at a time and adjust the counters/bar.
Reinforce that 'took away / left' does not automatically mean subtract — the structure of the story decides the operation.
Celebrate explanations that justify the operation from the situation, not from a single word.
activities.rationale: Concrete acting-out and drawing underpin the pictorial bar model and give young children a tangible way to represent an unknown before abstract equations. This supports the standards' call for concrete objects and pictorial representations.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
Bar/part-whole modelling makes the unknown visible and supports reasoning (including via the inverse) across all unknown positions; keyword strategies fail on missing-number problems.
learnerActions: Act out or draw the story with physical counters before choosing any operation.
Lay out a paper tape/bar strip and partition it into known parts and an unknown part to match the story.
Use an empty number line to count on and find a difference or an unknown.
Say aloud what you know, what you are trying to find, and why the operation you chose fits the story.
activities.intendedInsight: Modelling the situation with concrete materials — rather than matching keywords — reveals the correct operation even when the unknown is not the result.

activities.title: Coaching dialogue: 'What do we know, what are we finding?'
feedback: When a child applies an operation to the two given numbers automatically, without checking the story (e.g. trying 7 − 9 or 9 − 7 for 7 = ? − 9), redirect to the story structure with a question rather than giving the answer.
Follow the child's approach and ask for justification; adapt prompts to whether they are stuck on parsing '=' or on choosing the operation.
activities.rationale: Missing-number and start-unknown problems demand reasoning to an unknown; a Socratic dialogue may develop that reasoning by adapting to the child's approach. Dialogue complements, and does not replace, hands-on and pictorial modelling. This medium's efficacy is a proposal, not verified.
learnerActions: Respond to a coach who asks you to name what is known and what is unknown in a problem.
Justify which operation you will use and where the unknown sits, especially for start-unknown and missing-number problems.
Talk through 7 = ? − 9: identify that you need a starting number which, after removing 9, leaves 7.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasoning aloud about knowns and the unknown can develop the modelling and inverse reasoning needed for harder problem structures.

activities.title: Worked bar-model example with revealable steps
feedback: Prompt the learner to predict each next step before revealing it.
Ask them to point to where the unknown sits before the final number is shown.
activities.rationale: A static worked example anchors the pictorial modelling method and can be revisited; it cannot generate varied structures or let the child model their own problem, so it works best as a scaffold before or alongside the interactive builder.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve one-step addition and subtraction problems and missing-number problems such as 7 = ? − 9, using concrete objects and pictorial representations.
learnerActions: Study one worked problem shown with a bar model.
Reveal the solution steps one at a time and relate each step to the story.
Restate how the parts and whole map onto what the story gave and what it asked.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly worked bar model anchors the method and shows how the unknown is found from the known quantities: combining the parts when the whole is unknown, or taking a known part from the whole when a part is unknown.

activities.title: Missing-number and word-problem practice set
feedback: If a child answers 7 = ▢ − 9 as 7 − 9 or refuses, return to the bar model: whole ▢, parts 9 and 7, so ▢ = 16.

If a child subtracts on a take-away start-unknown problem (e.g. 'I had some, ate 9, 7 are left'), have them act it out to see that the start was larger than what remained. (On an add-on start-unknown problem such as 'I had some, got 5 more, now I have 12', subtracting 12 − 5 is correct.)
activities.rationale: Varied-position items probe the target directly and surface misconceptions, but practice/fill-in tasks present problems to solve and may not by themselves build the modelling process, so they belong after modelling work rather than before it.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.1: use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems with unknowns in all positions; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation.
learnerActions: Fill in equations with the unknown in different positions, e.g. 7 = ▢ − 9, ▢ + 5 = 12, 12 − ▢ = 8.
Answer word problems with picture support where the unknown is the result, change or start.
Mark which problems were 'find the start' problems rather than 'find what's left'.
activities.intendedInsight: Problems with the unknown in varied positions require the same modelling reasoning; recognising the structure matters more than the keyword.

constraints: Keep teaching modelling of the situation (act-out, drawing, bar/part-whole) over keyword strategies, extending the number range to 20.
Introduce the unknown in all positions (result, change, start) and use part-whole/bar models to make the unknown visible.
Connect missing-number problems to the inverse relationship and known bonds (7 = ? − 9 → ? = 16 via 7 + 9).
Have children place the unknown where it belongs in the equation, not always after the = sign.
Progress difficulty by problem STRUCTURE, not just larger numbers, and discuss why a chosen model fits the story.
Practice/fill-in items probe the target and surface misconceptions but do not by themselves build the modelling process; use them after hands-on and pictorial modelling.
A worked example is a scaffold: it anchors the method but cannot generate varied structures or let the child model their own problem.
Do not teach keyword-to-operation rules ('away/left' → subtract); these fail on start-unknown, change-unknown and missing-number problems.
Reading '=' as 'the answer goes here' causes children to reject missing-number forms; treat '=' relationally.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the diagnostic arithmetic: (1) 12 − 4 = 8 ✓; (2) start-unknown 'some cars, 5 drive away, 7 left' → start = 5 + 7 = 12 ✓; (3) 7 = ▢ − 9 → ▢ = 7 + 9 = 16 ✓. Added practice items also check out: ▢ + 5 = 12 → ▢ = 7; 12 − ▢ = 8 → ▢ = 4. These are used consistently in the activity feedback.

The source row lists two of three sources as verified:false (CCSS-M and the NCETM/IES bar-model claim). Comparative/efficacy framing from these should be treated as unverified; the rewrite scopes the 'interactive vs static', 'worked example' and 'dialogue' claims to stated affordances/limits rather than universal necessity or medium superiority.
The dialogue activity carries no sourceClaims because no listed source supports the efficacy of a Socratic dialogue medium; its benefit is stated as a proposal only.

The original rationale stated 'a static picture can't' generate varied structures and that a quiz 'presents problems rather than teaching'. These are retained only as qualified affordance/limit statements; a fixed example can still teach the method and practice items can still probe the target.
Independent re-audit confirms no learner-facing arithmetic, structural or contradiction errors; feedback remains coherent with the stated sweets example (whole = 16 from parts 9 and 7) throughout.

probeDeeper: In the cars problem, did the number of cars at the start get bigger or smaller after some drove away?
For 7 = ▢ − 9, what number do we start with so that taking 9 leaves 7?
How could counters or a bar help you see the cars problem?
Which of these was a 'find the start' problem, not a 'find what's left' problem?

errorPatterns.pattern: Keyword strategy — picks the operation from a word ('away/left' → subtract) regardless of structure, so start-unknown '5 drive away, 7 left' is computed as 7 − 5 or 5 − 7.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the situation with counters or a bar model before choosing an operation; do not teach keyword-to-operation rules.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child subtracts on the start-unknown problem (answers 2) instead of adding.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the missing-number equation left-to-right as 'compute the two numbers' — 7 = ▢ − 9 answered as 7 − 9 (or 'can't do it', or 2).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat = relationally with a part-whole / bar model (whole ▢, parts 9 and 7, so ▢ = 9 + 7).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives −2, 2, or refuses, treating ▢ as 'the answer of a sum'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Correct set-up but a counting / arithmetic slip within 20.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the calculation; the modelling and operation choice are sound, so do not reteach them.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Right operation and structure, answer off by one or two.

responseLevels.gap: Applies a keyword/default operation; cannot handle start-unknown or missing-number equations.
responseLevels.full: Models and solves varied structures within 20 — result-unknown, start-unknown, and missing-number equations — choosing the operation from the situation.
responseLevels.partial: Solves result-unknown problems reliably but defaults to subtracting on start-unknown, or cannot parse 7 = ▢ − 9.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Solve these — you can use counters. (1) I have 12 sweets and eat 4 — how many are left? (2) There were some cars; 5 drive away and 7 are left — how many were there at the start? (3) Fill the box: 7 = ▢ − 9.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three problems are deliberately different STRUCTURES (result-unknown is easy; start-unknown and the missing-minuend equation are hard — CGI/Carpenter). A keyword solver does 12 − 4 fine but subtracts on 'drive away' for the start-unknown and cannot handle 7 = ▢ − 9. Watch whether the child models the situation or grabs numbers plus a keyword.
